newsitem.title: CHINA: No immediate results from Sino-Europe talks on WTO.
newsitem.headline: No immediate results from Sino-Europe talks on WTO.

text.p: Chinese and European negotiators on Thursday ended four days of talks with no immediate progress on Beijing's plan to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), European Union officials said.

The EU had sought commitments from China on market access for services such as telecommunications, banking, insurance, news agencies and retailing, but Beijing's offered terms for WTO entry remained well short of requirements, they said.

"Discussions were open and constructive, even if they did not yield immediate results," the EU said in a statement that laid out in unusual detail the conditions attached by Europe to China's entry to the global trade club.
Much remained to be done to hammer out an adequate set of Chinese commitments, despite proposals from Beijing that kick-started the stalled accession process, the EU said.
Progress on trading rights issues had left the service sector as a key area of dispute.
"In this area, China had submitted an improved offer in November of last year, which however still remains well short of WTO standards," it said.
China has for years campaigned to be allowed to join the WTO and its predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but has failed to agree on terms with existing members.
Chinese Premier Li Peng said last week the accession delays were abnormal and left the WTO incomplete without one of the world's largest and fastest-growing economies.

Beijing wants to enjoy the favourable conditions accorded other developing countries, but some Western nations, the United States prominent among them, have argued that the Chinese economy is too big to be treated so leniently.

The Beijing talks had dealt extensively with European demands for improved access to China's markets for banking services, insurance, securities trading, maritime shipping including dredging and telecommunications, the EU said.

Brussels expected Chinese commitments to gradually allow foreign banking and insurance services to be offered to local consumers, entry for foreign securities companies and eased restrictions on foreign law firms, it said.
China should allow unrestricted establishment of shipping companies, the setting up of foreign wholesale and retail firms, establishment rights for news and travel agencies, it said.
The tightly guarded but fast-growing telecommunications sector should also be thrown open to foreign competition, it said -- a demand Beijing has repeatedly rejected in the past.
"In telecommunications a Chinese commitment should include network competition as well as resale, and (should) cover all technologies and types of service," the EU said.
European negotiators had highlighted the need for acceptance of a basic set of regulatory principles for the sector, including an independent regulator, it said.
Premier Li last week reaffirmed Beijing's enthusiasm for WTO entry, despite condemning delays as abnormal.
"China is a major trading country and would very much like to join this organisation," Li said. "Not only does the WTO need China, but China also needs the WTO."
